newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CVRD - The business of iron ore mining.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CVRD - The business of iron ore mining.

text.p: Control of the largest iron ore deposit in the world is up for grabs Tuesday when Brazil's government auctions a 40-45 percent voting stake in minig giant CVRD for a base price of 3 billion reais ($2.83 billion).

The company is the world's largest iron ore producer and exporter and its Carajas mining district in the northern state of Para is home to 18 billion tonnes of iron ore, the prize everyone is after at the auction.

CVRD produces more than 100 million tonnes of iron ore a year, and sells 35 percent of output to Japan, China and Korea, 25 percent to Europe, six percent to the United States and four percent to Africa and the Middle East.
CVRD, which posted a 1996 profit of $632 million, has total assets of $10.4 billion and annual sales of $5 billion.

During its 55-year existence as a state-owned compnay, CVRD has developed into a major conglomerate with more than 15,400 employees and 44 subsidiaries which control all aspects of the business from mining to production to transport.

CVRD owns two railways, which transport 150 million tonnes of cargo per year, and a shipping company, Vale do Rio Doce Navegacao SA (Docenave), which transports 96.32 million tonnes of cargo per year across the world.
In total, CVRD has iron ore reserves of 41.5 billion tonnes, enough to secure 400 years of production, and Carajas is not only rich in iron ore, but also in other metals.
CVRD is also Latin America's largest producer of gold with output of 18 tonnes per year and proven reserves of 106.4 tonnes. By the year 2001, CVRD expects to produce 31 tonnes of gold per year.
The company's gold fortunes could be considerably higher, however, if a new gold deposit found at Serra Leste in the Carajas region in 1995 proves to hold an estimated 150 tonnes of gold.

Carajas has become CVRD's most promising mining project since it was discovered in 1972. It began operations in 1985, with annual output and exports of more than 40 million tonnes of iron ore, one million tonnes of manganese and growing quantities of gold and other metals.
The Salobo mines located in the Carajas region are expected to produce an annual 300,000 tonnes of copper, 14 tonnes of silver and three tonnes of gold by 2001.

The company has also hit the headlines in recent months with news of other potentially huge gold finds in Carajas, but has consistently maintained that it is premature to speak of any significant discoveries.

Apart from its mining interests, CVRD has significant pulp and paper operations in the state of Bahia with a forested area of 315,000 hectares and a capacity to produce 1.2 million tonnes of pulp and 250,000 tonnes of paper per year.

The company's Celmar joint venture in northeastern Maranhao state, due to come online in 2001, is expected to produce an annual 500,000 tonnes of pulp, making it the second largest pulp producer in Brazil. It is located on 138,000 hectares of forest.
CVRD's wealth is being sold off in three stages starting with the April 29 auction, followed by a staff and global offer later in the year.

The sale is Latin America's biggest privatization to date and expected to net the government at least $5 billion, that is $2 billion more than the previous record privatization of Argentine oil giant YPF.
